nodes.title: Sol 8: Sweeping the Solar Farm
nodes.nasaFactBanner: 2018 LESSON: Opportunity had to wait for wind, but crews can sweep panels themselves.
nodes.storyText: Dust is finally settling! Opportunity rover had to wait for dust devils to clean it. Your crew can put on dustproof suits and sweep panels!
nodes.guideTip: Solar panels need clean glass. Dust blocks the light, just like a dirty window!
nodes.novaHint: Sunlight is coming back. Think about what helps you use it best.

consequences.text: Sol 4 cold fuel uses power (-5% Power), but lifts morale (+3% Crew Health).
Sol 7 cold ration bars saved power (0% Electricity Conserved!), but tired everyone (-5% Crew Health).
Your Sol 7 orbital scan found sunny gaps in the haze (0% Electricity Conserved!).
Clean water loops help everyone feel good (+4% Crew Health), but pumps use power (-3% Power).
Clean rover plugs help power (0% Electricity Conserved!), but suits tired the crew (-3% Crew Health).

choiceA.description: Two astronauts go outside with dust shields to clean Wing Array 1.
choiceA.outcomeText: Sunlight pours onto clean solar glass! Your spacewalkers return proud, sore, and dusty.
choiceA.nasaRealDecision: Mars storms fade slowly. Sunlight returns, but dust can still cling to panels.
choiceA.nasaFactEmphasis: Panels make power only when sunlight gets through and the glass is clean.
choiceA.guideReaction: Whoa, clean panels! More power, but sore astronauts. Great trade!

choiceB.description: Tired astronauts sleep indoors while batteries are balanced.
choiceB.outcomeText: Rest heals aching backs. The dusty panels waste some of the returning sun.
choiceB.nasaRealDecision: In 2018, dust in the air held in heat at night. Crews could use less heater power.
choiceB.nasaFactEmphasis: Mars air is very thin, and nights can drop to -90°F.
choiceB.guideReaction: Hmm, rest feels great! Dusty panels still miss that sunshine, though.

choiceC.description: A quick shift clears frost from radiator pipes and fixes loose wires.
choiceC.outcomeText: Tighter wires waste less power. The cold dust chills the repair team.
choiceC.nasaComparisonTitle: Nuclear Power Works in the Dark
choiceC.nasaRealDecision: Opportunity ran on solar power and went quiet. Curiosity kept going on nuclear power.
choiceC.nasaFactEmphasis: A nuclear core can make electricity even when the sky is dark.
choiceC.guideReaction: Nice fix! Less wasted power, but brrr, the crew is chilly.

nodes.title: Sol 8: Sunlight Returns
nodes.nasaFactBanner: 2018 LESSON: Cleaning sticky dust off panels is the fastest way to get power back.
nodes.storyText: Sunlight is back, but sticky red dust covers your panels and greenhouse glass. Opportunity waited for wind to clean it. You can choose how to clean up or rest.
nodes.guideTip: Mars dust is sticky like a balloon rubbed on hair. Static makes it cling!
nodes.novaHint: Cleaning costs effort and rest costs power. Which matters more right now?

consequences.text: Sol 7 skylight sweeping gives power (+3% Electricity), but sore muscles slow everyone (-4% Crew Health).
Backup oxygen from Sol 1 keeps the air fresh during cleanup (+4% Crew Health).
Portable scrubbers use steady power (-3% Power) but protect lungs (+4% Crew Health).
Sol 7 hot meals gave energy (+4% Crew Health), but used power (-3% Power).
Your Sol 7 air purge cleared lungs (+5% Crew Health), but left batteries lower (-4% Power).

choiceA.description: Shaker frames rattle the solar farm and knock the dust off.
choiceA.outcomeText: Sheets of dust slide off the panels! The buzzing noise makes sleeping hard.
choiceA.nasaRealDecision: Mars storms fade slowly. Sunlight returns, but dust can still cling to panels.
choiceA.nasaFactEmphasis: Panels make power only when sunlight gets through and the glass is clean.
choiceA.guideReaction: Rattle, rattle! Clean panels, but the noise is tiring.

choiceB.description: Use steady power to moisten dry air and let everyone sleep.
choiceB.outcomeText: Deep sleep and moist air help the crew. Battery power drops a bit.
choiceB.nasaRealDecision: NASA is testing dust shields and suit doors that keep sticky Mars dust outside.
choiceB.nasaFactEmphasis: Mars dust clings like static and can harm lungs indoors.
choiceB.guideReaction: Aah, sleepy time! The crew feels great, and power dips.

choiceC.description: Link the Chariot Rover and zap dust off the panels.
choiceC.outcomeText: Dust shields clear the panels with no spacewalk. Watching the power link tires everyone.
choiceC.nasaRealDecision: Mars storms fade slowly. Sunlight returns, but dust can still cling to panels.
choiceC.nasaFactEmphasis: Panels make power only when sunlight gets through and the glass is clean.
choiceC.guideReaction: Zap! Power is up, and nobody had to spacewalk. Cool!

nodes.title: Sol 8: Cooling Pump Trouble
nodes.nasaFactBanner: 2018 LESSON: Real power machines need safety room, not nonstop top speed.
nodes.storyText: Curiosity's nuclear power has no moving parts. Your reactor cooling pump just broke! Overhead, dust once over 37 miles high is finally sinking.
nodes.guideTip: Pumps move cool liquid past the hot reactor. When a pump breaks, we need a plan!
nodes.novaHint: A broken part is a problem, but your crew still needs care too.

consequences.text: Pushing the core hard on Sol 6 hurt a cooling seal (-6% Power).
Shaken panels add fresh power (+3% Electricity), but the noise stressed the crew (-4% Crew Health).
Wearing helmets indoors since Sol 7 left the crew sore and thirsty (-6% Crew Health).
Heated radar gears stay ice-free (0% Electricity Conserved!), but chilly rooms stiffen joints (-3% Crew Health).

choiceA.description: Use stored power for oxygen, warm water, and rest.
choiceA.outcomeText: Sick-bay mist revives the crew fast. Your power reserves fall very low.
choiceA.nasaRealDecision: In 2018, the storm lifted water vapor high above Mars. Future bases will recycle every drop.
choiceA.nasaFactEmphasis: Space stations already recycle water, and Mars bases will need to as well.
choiceA.guideReaction: Healing time! The crew feels much better, but power is low.

choiceB.description: Spend power and energy to launch a balloon that studies the storm.
choiceB.outcomeText: Your balloon sends great storm data to NASA. It also strains the crew and power.
choiceB.nasaComparisonTitle: Orbiters Help Mars Talk to Earth
choiceB.nasaRealDecision: In 2018, NASA's Mars orbiter watched the storm grow. It also relays rover radio to Earth.
choiceB.nasaFactEmphasis: Radio messages take about 22 minutes to cross space.
choiceB.guideReaction: Great science! Hmm, it wore everyone out. Rest helps next time.

choiceC.description: Tired engineers crawl through tunnels to join rover pumps to the reactor.
choiceC.outcomeText: The bypass steadies reactor power. The tight tunnels leave bruises and tired muscles.
choiceC.nasaRealDecision: In 2018, the storm lifted water vapor high above Mars. Future bases will recycle every drop.
choiceC.nasaFactEmphasis: Space stations already recycle water, and Mars bases will need to as well.
choiceC.guideReaction: Clever fix! Hmm, crawling tunnels hurts. Take care of your crew.

nodes.title: Sol 8: Sky Maps and Fuel
nodes.nasaFactBanner: 2018 LESSON: Sky maps from orbit help crews plan solar recovery and protect fuel.
nodes.storyText: A relay satellite sends you clearing-sky maps. Radio takes about 22 minutes to reach Earth. Chillers that keep rocket fuel cold now compete with base repairs.
nodes.guideTip: Satellites circle Mars and take pictures from above. They show where the sky is clearing!
nodes.novaHint: Fuel, power, and crew all need care. What will you protect first?

consequences.text: Sol 7's scan found thin clouds over Ares Base (0% Electricity Conserved!).
Melted ice keeps heaters running (-4% Power) and flasks full (+5% Crew Health).
Your drone map helps field checks (0% Electricity Conserved!), but needs focus (-2% Crew Health).
Sealing the dusty lab helps breathing (+3% Crew Health), but uses power (-3% Power).

choiceA.description: Astronauts go out to tilt solar wings toward sunny spots.
choiceA.outcomeText: Tilted towers catch the returning sun right away. The dusty wind chills the crew.
choiceA.nasaRealDecision: Mars storms fade slowly. Sunlight returns, but dust can still cling to panels.
choiceA.nasaFactEmphasis: Panels make power only when sunlight gets through and the glass is clean.
choiceA.guideReaction: Smart aiming! More power, but brrr, the crew is cold.

choiceB.description: Leave the towers alone and clean water and warm bunks.
choiceB.outcomeText: Fresh water and cozy bunks rebuild energy. The power gauge dips down.
choiceB.nasaRealDecision: In 2018, the storm lifted water vapor high above Mars. Future bases will recycle every drop.
choiceB.nasaFactEmphasis: Space stations already recycle water, and Mars bases will need to as well.
choiceB.guideReaction: Yum, clean water! The crew feels good, and power dips.

choiceC.description: Spend dish power on recovery plans and video letters from Earth.
choiceC.outcomeText: Seeing smiling families brightens the whole base. Smart checklists are ready too.
choiceC.nasaComparisonTitle: Orbiters Help Mars Talk to Earth
choiceC.nasaRealDecision: In 2018, NASA's Mars orbiter watched the storm grow. It also relays rover radio to Earth.
choiceC.nasaFactEmphasis: Radio messages take about 22 minutes to cross space.
choiceC.guideReaction: Hello, Earth! Happy faces boost the crew, and power dips.

nodes.title: Sol 9: Prepare the Rocket
nodes.nasaFactBanner: 2018 LESSON: In July 2018, NASA listened daily for Opportunity as skies brightened.
nodes.storyText: Warm golden light returns! Opportunity stayed silent in 2018, but you can power MOXIE oxygen makers. Chillers can again keep rocket fuel cold for the trip home.
nodes.guideTip: MOXIE makes oxygen from Mars air. Power from sunshine lets it run again!
nodes.novaHint: Sunshine is back. Think about what your crew and rocket need most.

consequences.text: Swept Wing 1 gives morning power (+3% Electricity), but sore workers need rest (-4% Crew Health).
Warm kitchens use steady power (-3% Power), but well-fed astronauts stay strong (+4% Crew Health).
Clean water from Sol 7 keeps everyone ready for pre-launch checks (+4% Crew Health).
Good sleep made the crew stronger (+5% Crew Health), but used some power (-4% Power).
Tilted towers catch extra morning power (+3% Electricity), but tired the crew (-3% Crew Health).

choiceA.description: Use solar power to split water ice into oxygen and clean water.
choiceA.outcomeText: Fresh oxygen and clean water fill Ares Base. Your crew is ready for Sol 10!
choiceA.nasaRealDecision: In 2018, the storm lifted water vapor high above Mars. Future bases will recycle every drop.
choiceA.nasaFactEmphasis: Space stations already recycle water, and Mars bases will need to as well.
choiceA.guideReaction: Deep breaths! The crew is strong, and power is lower.

choiceB.description: The crew works overtime to test the fuel chillers and power.
choiceB.outcomeText: The chillers run smoothly and power climbs. Long checklists tire the astronauts.
choiceB.nasaRealDecision: Mars return rockets may use liquid fuel that must stay very cold. Cooling takes steady power.
choiceB.nasaFactEmphasis: Liquid oxygen boils away if it gets warm, so rockets need cooling.
choiceB.guideReaction: Chill, rocket, chill! More power, but the crew is tired.

choiceC.description: A team crosses the dunes to reconnect backup solar cables.
choiceC.outcomeText: Extra panels send steady power home. Trudging in bulky suits tires everyone.
choiceC.nasaRealDecision: Mars storms fade slowly. Sunlight returns, but dust can still cling to panels.
choiceC.nasaFactEmphasis: Panels make power only when sunlight gets through and the glass is clean.
choiceC.guideReaction: Long hike, big reward! More power, and sleepy legs.

nodes.title: Sol 9: Clear Skies, Cold Nights
nodes.nasaFactBanner: 2018 LESSON: As dust settled in July 2018, Mars nights got very cold again.
nodes.storyText: Without dust to hold in heat, nights fall to -90°F again! Mars has very thin air, so frost builds on radiators. Your airlock suits help with outside jobs.
nodes.guideTip: Thin air can't hold much heat. That is why Mars gets so cold at night!
nodes.novaHint: Cold nights ask a lot from people and machines. Plan for both.

consequences.text: Sealed corridors save power (0% Electricity Conserved!), but icy doorways stiffen joints (-4% Crew Health).
Radio silence kept batteries full (0% Electricity Conserved!), but the crew feels lonely (-4% Crew Health).
Shaken panels give crisp morning power (+3% Electricity), but vibration bothers sleep (-3% Crew Health).
Rest steadied the crew (+4% Crew Health), but dusty panels slowed charging (-3% Power).
Shaken panels raised charging (+3% Electricity), but the buzzing hurt sleep (-3% Crew Health).
Sick-bay care lifted weak crew (+5% Crew Health), but drained power overnight (-4% Power).

choiceA.description: Suited astronauts go out in the -90°F evening to scrape ice from radiators.
choiceA.outcomeText: Clean radiators cool better and save power. The frosty work leaves the crew worn out.
choiceA.nasaRealDecision: In 2018, the storm lifted water vapor high above Mars. Future bases will recycle every drop.
choiceA.nasaFactEmphasis: Space stations already recycle water, and Mars bases will need to as well.
choiceA.guideReaction: Chip, chip! Radiators work better, but the crew is freezing.

choiceB.description: Run the heaters high while doctors check all four astronauts.
choiceB.outcomeText: Warm checkups lift everyone's health. The battery meters drop down.
choiceB.nasaRealDecision: Astronauts on the space station grow salad plants under colorful LED lights.
choiceB.nasaFactEmphasis: Fresh plants give vitamins and cheer, but grow lights use steady power.
choiceB.guideReaction: Doctor time! Healthy crew, lower power. A fair trade.

choiceC.description: Heaters melt ice slowly while the crew balances power circuits.
choiceC.outcomeText: Careful work saves reserve power. Missing sleep leaves the crew weary before Sol 10.
choiceC.nasaRealDecision: In 2018, the storm lifted water vapor high above Mars. Future bases will recycle every drop.
choiceC.nasaFactEmphasis: Space stations already recycle water, and Mars bases will need to as well.
choiceC.guideReaction: Good teamwork! Power is steadier, but everyone needs sleep.

nodes.title: Sol 9: Survival Mode
nodes.nasaFactBanner: 2018 LESSON: After big storms, NASA checks spacecraft health before a full restart.
nodes.storyText: A 22-minute radio delay can't stop good news! A relay satellite brings alerts from Mission Control. One Sol is left: help the crew, send science, or seal the reactor bay.
nodes.guideTip: Mission Control is on Earth. The relay satellite carries their messages to you.
nodes.novaHint: One Sol is left. Think about what you can't get back later.

consequences.text: The Sol 8 bypass leaks power (-5% Power) and hums by the bunks (-3% Crew Health).
Dust from Sol 5 still irritates dry throats in the shelter (-5% Crew Health).
Rover-cleaned panels give bonus daylight power (+3% Electricity), but screens tire eyes (-2% Crew Health).
The storm balloon timed skies (0% Electricity Conserved!), but outdoor duties tired everyone (-4% Crew Health).
Clean water and rest steadied everyone (+4% Crew Health), but power dropped (-4% Power).

choiceA.description: Spend battery power on cabin cleaning, warm water, and medical rest.
choiceA.outcomeText: Cabin air turns spotless and the crew rallies. Battery reserves dip very low.
choiceA.nasaRealDecision: NASA is testing dust shields and suit doors that keep sticky Mars dust outside.
choiceA.nasaFactEmphasis: Mars dust clings like static and can harm lungs indoors.
choiceA.guideReaction: Sparkly clean! The crew is strong, but power is quite low.

choiceB.description: Spend power and focus to upload your storm data and lock the latches.
choiceB.outcomeText: Earth gets every bit of your storm data. The base and crew feel stretched.
choiceB.nasaComparisonTitle: Orbiters Help Mars Talk to Earth
choiceB.nasaRealDecision: In 2018, NASA's Mars orbiter watched the storm grow. It also relays rover radio to Earth.
choiceB.nasaFactEmphasis: Radio messages take about 22 minutes to cross space.
choiceB.guideReaction: Science sent! Hmm, you are running low. Rest helps.

choiceC.description: Seal the outer doors to keep heat in and save power.
choiceC.outcomeText: Sealed doors stop wasted power. Sleeping side by side tires the crew.
choiceC.nasaComparisonTitle: Nuclear Power Works in the Dark
choiceC.nasaRealDecision: Opportunity ran on solar power and went quiet. Curiosity kept going on nuclear power.
choiceC.nasaFactEmphasis: A nuclear core can make electricity even when the sky is dark.
choiceC.guideReaction: Snug and safe! Power is saved, but it is a squeeze.

nodes.title: Sol 9: Rovers and Greenhouse
nodes.nasaFactBanner: 2018 LESSON: Clearing dust fast helps solar and nuclear bases bounce back.
nodes.storyText: No need to wait for dust devils! You can revive greenhouse crops and water tanks.
nodes.guideTip: A greenhouse gives fresh food. Recycling water means no drop is wasted!
nodes.novaHint: You have a strong team. Think about which job helps the most.

consequences.text: Cleared arrays give morning power (+3% Electricity), but scrubbing rover plugs tired everyone (-3% Crew Health).
Smart checklists from Sol 8 trim wasted power (0% Electricity Conserved!).
Linked rover batteries share power (0% Electricity Conserved!), but heavy cables need care (-2% Crew Health).
Scraped radiators help heat flow (0% Electricity Conserved!), but cold aches linger (-3% Crew Health).
The reactor bypass saved power (0% Electricity Conserved!), but loud pumps rattled bunks (-4% Crew Health).

choiceA.description: Line up solar trackers and turn on dust shields before dawn.
choiceA.outcomeText: Every solar wing locks onto the bright Sun. The heavy outdoor work strains the crew.
choiceA.nasaRealDecision: Mars storms fade slowly. Sunlight returns, but dust can still cling to panels.
choiceA.nasaFactEmphasis: Panels make power only when sunlight gets through and the glass is clean.
choiceA.guideReaction: Sun, here we come! Power is up, and the crew is tired.

choiceB.description: Use daylight power to flush water tanks and light the veggie racks.
choiceB.outcomeText: Green sprouts and fresh water lift the crew fast. It costs a fair bit of power.
choiceB.nasaRealDecision: Astronauts on the space station grow salad plants under colorful LED lights.
choiceB.nasaFactEmphasis: Fresh plants give vitamins and cheer, but grow lights use steady power.
choiceB.guideReaction: Yum, fresh veggies! The crew feels great, and power dips.

choiceC.description: Send extra rover and core power into the return rocket overnight.
choiceC.outcomeText: The rocket batteries fill up safely. Night checks cut the crew's sleep.
choiceC.nasaComparisonTitle: Nuclear Power Works in the Dark
choiceC.nasaRealDecision: Opportunity ran on solar power and went quiet. Curiosity kept going on nuclear power.
choiceC.nasaFactEmphasis: A nuclear core can make electricity even when the sky is dark.
choiceC.guideReaction: Rocket charged! Power is up, but sleepy astronauts need rest.

nodes.title: Sol 10: Dawn After the Storm
nodes.nasaFactBanner: 2018 LESSON: Mars storms fade slowly over weeks, so teamwork matters at the end.
nodes.storyText: Sunlight floods Ares Base on your tenth Martian Sol! Your nuclear power core hums beside the solar wings. One last choice: keep rocket fuel cold or help the crew.
nodes.guideTip: Ten Sols! The storm is nearly over, and your base made it. Wow!
nodes.novaHint: This is your final push. Think about what gets everyone home strong.

consequences.text: Refilled water and oxygen keep everyone alert (+4% Crew Health), but used power (-3% Power).
Clear radiators work better (0% Electricity Conserved!), but icy work left crew sore (-3% Crew Health).
Tuned trackers catch strong sun (+3% Electricity), but dune hikes tired the crew (-3% Crew Health).

choiceA.description: The crew inspects outside to max the battery vaults and rocket chillers.
choiceA.outcomeText: Chillers and batteries glow green, ready for liftoff! Your astronauts finish tired but proud.
choiceA.nasaRealDecision: Mars return rockets may use liquid fuel that must stay very cold. Cooling takes steady power.
choiceA.nasaFactEmphasis: Liquid oxygen boils away if it gets warm, so rockets need cooling.
choiceA.guideReaction: Rocket ready! The crew is worn out, but so proud.

choiceB.description: Use leftover power for plant lights and a warm crew meal.
choiceB.outcomeText: Astronauts cheer around glowing green sprouts. Power dips, but spirits soar!
choiceB.nasaRealDecision: Astronauts on the space station grow salad plants under colorful LED lights.
choiceB.nasaFactEmphasis: Fresh plants give vitamins and cheer, but grow lights use steady power.
choiceB.guideReaction: Feast time! Cheers all around, and a happy crew!

choiceC.description: Astronauts test cables joining rover panels to the nuclear power bus.
choiceC.outcomeText: Nuclear and solar lines give rock-steady power. Long suit shifts tire the crew.
choiceC.nasaComparisonTitle: Nuclear Power Works in the Dark
choiceC.nasaRealDecision: Opportunity ran on solar power and went quiet. Curiosity kept going on nuclear power.
choiceC.nasaFactEmphasis: A nuclear core can make electricity even when the sky is dark.
choiceC.guideReaction: Team power! Steady and strong, with one tired crew.

nodes.title: Sol 10: The Final Check
nodes.nasaFactBanner: 2018 LESSON: Opportunity went silent in 2018, so power reserves decide survival.
nodes.storyText: Skies glow gold again. Opportunity ran out of power with no dust-devil cleaning. Finish checking your crew and the lines that keep rocket fuel cold!
nodes.guideTip: Opportunity's batteries ran low, so it went quiet. Yours are still going!
nodes.novaHint: The finish line is close. Pick the check that makes your base strongest.

consequences.text: Tested chillers locked power buses (0% Electricity Conserved!), but late shifts tired everyone (-3% Crew Health).
Checkups and rest boosted readiness (+5% Crew Health), but trimmed the battery (-4% Power).
Clean airlocks cleared storm dust (+4% Crew Health), but filters use power (-3% Power).

choiceA.description: Suit up one last time to reset and clean outside solar inverters.
choiceA.outcomeText: Clean solar power refills the grid and the meters surge! The crew is spent at the finish line.
choiceA.nasaRealDecision: Mars storms fade slowly. Sunlight returns, but dust can still cling to panels.
choiceA.nasaFactEmphasis: Panels make power only when sunlight gets through and the glass is clean.
choiceA.guideReaction: Power surge! Meters are up, and the crew is very tired.

choiceB.description: Use power indoors to clear dust from vents and check the crew.
choiceB.outcomeText: Medical monitors flash healthy green for all four astronauts. Power gauges dip a little.
choiceB.nasaRealDecision: NASA is testing dust shields and suit doors that keep sticky Mars dust outside.
choiceB.nasaFactEmphasis: Mars dust clings like static and can harm lungs indoors.
choiceB.guideReaction: Green lights for all four! Healthy crew, ready to go home!

choiceC.description: Warm the cabin while automatic checks inspect the return fuel tanks.
choiceC.outcomeText: The crew relaxes while the rocket gets checked. Battery bars look a bit lighter.
choiceC.nasaRealDecision: Mars return rockets may use liquid fuel that must stay very cold. Cooling takes steady power.
choiceC.nasaFactEmphasis: Liquid oxygen boils away if it gets warm, so rockets need cooling.
choiceC.guideReaction: Rocket checked! Relaxed crew, a bit less power.

nodes.title: Sol 10: The Rescue Moment
nodes.nasaFactBanner: 2018 LESSON: Early warnings in 2018 showed why power must never hit zero.
nodes.storyText: Satellites spotted a small dust storm early, but your base runs low. Make one last trade with your airlock suits. Radio replies take 22 minutes, so decide now!
nodes.guideTip: Warnings help! Satellites saw the 2018 storm start long before it covered Mars.
nodes.novaHint: Your reserves are low. Think about what keeps the crew safe and hopeful.

consequences.text: Uploading storm science drained batteries (-3% Power), but NASA's cheers lifted spirits (+2% Crew Health).
Fresh greens and mineral water renewed strength (+5% Crew Health), but power dipped (-4% Power).

choiceA.description: Pour leftover battery power into oxygen masks and warm blankets.
choiceA.outcomeText: Every astronaut breathes easy until the skies clear. The machines get less power.
choiceA.nasaRealDecision: NASA's MOXIE made oxygen from Mars air on the Perseverance rover.
choiceA.nasaFactEmphasis: Mars air is mostly carbon dioxide, and MOXIE turns some into oxygen.
choiceA.guideReaction: Breathe easy! The crew is safe, and the base is low.

choiceB.description: Turn off cabin heat to save electronics and signal the orbiter.
choiceB.outcomeText: Your beacon reaches the satellites! The chilly astronauts snuggle into sleep pods.
choiceB.nasaComparisonTitle: Orbiters Help Mars Talk to Earth
choiceB.nasaRealDecision: In 2018, NASA's Mars orbiter watched the storm grow. It also relays rover radio to Earth.
choiceB.nasaFactEmphasis: Radio messages take about 22 minutes to cross space.
choiceB.guideReaction: Signal sent! Brrr, the crew is cold, but power is saved.

choiceC.description: Pulse dust shields so the morning sun can charge Ares Base.
choiceC.outcomeText: Clean glass drinks in the dawn sunlight! The long control shifts tire the crew.
choiceC.nasaRealDecision: Mars storms fade slowly. Sunlight returns, but dust can still cling to panels.
choiceC.nasaFactEmphasis: Panels make power only when sunlight gets through and the glass is clean.
choiceC.guideReaction: Dawn power! Panels glow, and the crew has earned a nap.

nodes.title: Sol 10: Ready for Liftoff
nodes.nasaFactBanner: 2018 LESSON: Nuclear plus solar power helps Mars crews finish storms ready to fly.
nodes.storyText: Curiosity kept going through 2018's dust, and your base shines too! Skies are sunny again. Send power to launch, or restore greenhouse plants and water recycling.
nodes.guideTip: Two power sources made your base strong. Sun and nuclear are great teammates!
nodes.novaHint: Liftoff is near. Think about what your crew needs for a hopeful finish.

consequences.text: Ridge panels bring morning power (+3% Electricity), but dune hikes tired the crew (-3% Crew Health).
Double shifts balanced the batteries (0% Electricity Conserved!), but wore down the crew (-4% Crew Health).
Emergency seals kept backup power (0% Electricity Conserved!), but cramped the crew (-4% Crew Health).
Charged rocket capacitors steadied launch systems (0% Electricity Conserved!), but cost sleep (-3% Crew Health).

choiceA.description: The crew checks cables outside to push extra power into launch batteries.
choiceA.outcomeText: Launch batteries leap to high voltage, ready for liftoff! The crew is drained but cheering.
choiceA.nasaRealDecision: Mars storms fade slowly. Sunlight returns, but dust can still cling to panels.
choiceA.nasaFactEmphasis: Panels make power only when sunlight gets through and the glass is clean.
choiceA.guideReaction: Launch ready! Power is high, and one very proud crew!

choiceB.description: Use daylight power for fresh veggies, clean water, and a rest shift.
choiceB.outcomeText: Bright grow-lights and clean water lift every spirit. Mission Control is about to log your score!
choiceB.nasaRealDecision: Astronauts on the space station grow salad plants under colorful LED lights.
choiceB.nasaFactEmphasis: Fresh plants give vitamins and cheer, but grow lights use steady power.
choiceB.guideReaction: Fresh and happy! A hopeful crew is ready for home!

choiceC.description: Warm the crew quarters during the last automatic fuel checks.
choiceC.outcomeText: The crew rests easy during final checks. Battery storage dips gently.
choiceC.nasaRealDecision: Mars return rockets may use liquid fuel that must stay very cold. Cooling takes steady power.
choiceC.nasaFactEmphasis: Liquid oxygen boils away if it gets warm, so rockets need cooling.
choiceC.guideReaction: Cozy finish! Rested crew, and power only dips a little.
